comments.text:
Hi,
I really like your videos and the new information you provide in reviews.

But I have some tips, how you can improve the flow of these videos.
- don't read information like core count or fps numbers that are written on screen. If we want that information, we can read it ourselves. Instead provide extra information. (I can't comprehend the fps numbers anyway, if your that fast.)
 (I noticed this also in the last review. The video was long, because you talked too much about information that was printed on screen.)
- instead of reading out to fps numbers (60 vs 80), give the relative improvement (+33%). It is easier to get a full picture between multiple games). If we want the numbers we can pause.
- instead of putting 0 fps on a chart. Put dnf (did not finish).
- instead of zooming in on an existing chart, create a new one. It is easier to see, what you want to emphasize.
- Seeing all relevant gpus in 1 graph is nice but confusing. Maybe provide 2 grpahs, 1 with all gpus and one with the "relevant" ones. (3060, 4060, 3070, 7600 XT)
- Color the names of the gpus by manufacturer (AMD red, nvidia green, intel blue). So we can read these massive charts better.
- Emphasise the general gpu name instead of the exact model e.g. "AMD 7600 XT (Sapphire Pulse)" instead of "Sapphire 7600 XT Pulse" or put the exact name below in grey. This way its easier to find models you are searching.

Please continue making great videos

It really confuses me why people are critisiing bottom end cards for not being able to play 4k epic settings..... Its a bottom end card it shouldnt be expected to.

On the flip side i totally disagree with these cards being sold as gaming cards at all. unless they match or exceed the current generation console in feature set (so 16gb of memory) they can not be considered a current generation gaming card. The console set the base line as the developers develop to target the consoles. then selling them with essentially the same name as the higher memory counterparts is just out right criminal.

But we should be real and expect bottom end performance from a bottom end card. if it can match console its bottom end current generation. these days thats arguably 60fps at 1080 with upscaling and frame gen at a minimum. If it cant do this its not a viable product for the target market.

on modern titles with 4k and maxed out settings, these should really only be considered a stress test or a performance benchmark for top end enthusiast cards, not mainstream. Most people dont have the display never mind the gpu to push 4k maxed out. its an interesting test to see how badly 8gb fails but 8gb was never a valid product anyway after consoles jumped to 16.

comments.text:
I appreciate the review Jay, but I think many card reviewers have lost the sauce when it comes to budget gaming.  You live in a world with common access to high power cards, which gives you a biased view on what is 'acceptable.'  Something like 50% of PC gamers have cards with 8GB or less.  Not everyone cares about super high quality visuals.  Graphics aren't the game, the actual game-play is what matters.  People on low end cards tend to be perfectly happy dropping graphics to get 60 fps, or going full gumby mode to run higher FPS.  Seeing someone get upset they can't run a budget card at max settings just makes them look entitled.
  
Nvidia deserves all the criticism it is getting surrounding issues with the 5000 series cards.  That doesn't make it correct to review cards in a way that is not representative of the way they will be used by the people that would actually get them.  Why ultra-high graphics presets? Why is no DLSS being used?  Somebody actually buying a 5060 is probably going to use DLSS in addition to running lower settings.


Benchmarking without upscaling is supposed to be about making the compute performance comparable between cards with different software capabilities, but it should not replace the real world usage that can be had when using those capabilities in the way actual people do.  The only people I know not running DLSS/Upscaling are the people buying the very high end cards.  Take that 5060, load up Borderlands 3 at 1440p or 1080p, medium presets, DLSS/upscaling set to balanced.  Look at the numbers.  Ask yourself:  Is this actually so bad?  Does it let you reasonably play games?  Does it keep the barrier to entry for PC gaming low?  With some self reflection you may be surprised at how usable you find these cards.

comments.text:
Controversial opinions. 
First, there is A LOT WRONG with the MSRP of such 8GB VRAM cards, both at nVidia and AMD, but there is nothing wrong with 8GB VRAM on a card. It is the new entry level, where years ago it was 4Gb. and it should be tested as such as well besides the apples to apples comparisons. 
Secondly, performance and Texture settings. 8Gb VRAM in 2025 is like the old 4Gb VRAM entry level cards, that low amount is and was never meant to game at MAX Texture settings or at resolution higher then 1440p. Back in those day we had to lower Texture quality (low medium) to remain within VRAM budget of our cards. Especially when going up a resolution from 1080 to 1440p.
Thirdly, games (old and new) have gotten spoiled by the marketing of the new graphics engines used and the graphical fidelity they can produce. It does not help that 24Gb VRAM HALO GPU's are used by developers to develop these games.. There is NO consideration or resource budgets anymore so it seems. This paints a wrong picture when previews or reviews are done, ppl now expect certain visual fidelity at certain performance within a certain budget.
Forthly, latest graphics engines. Create tremendous graphical fidelity, at a very high cost of performance. Even on the lowest settings or latest gen entry level hardware and THAT should be LOUDLY criticized by anyone and reviewers alike. It sets a bad president and course. It artificially pushes consumers to stretch their budgets or FOMO them into the HOLA segment. But this is a chicken and egg thing.


Anyway, end or rant.

I am not a gamer anymore, but I was building a desktop (I haven't had one in probably 20-25 years, I always played on laptops), and I thought that the 3060 Ti that I had at hand was probably not powerful enough, especially for the monitor I just bought.

JFC this is madness. Almost all cards cost twice as much as their MSRP, if they are even available, and apparently you nowadays need to rent your kidney to be able to play Minecraft in normal resolution.
Game companies have just given up trying to optimize in the slightest.
Anyway, I was looking at a 7800XTX for 1000, which was pretty close to MSRP, and my other candidate was the 9070 XT, which was supposed to be 600, but everywhere was almost 1000 like the 7800XTX.
By pure luck, I found actually a 9070XT at 730 which is according to some reviews I have read is the "actual MSRP", so I am very happy with it.
For context, my 3060 Ti is in the box, completely new, not even the seals have been broken. I went to check in Amazon out of curiosity, and the very same model is being sold for 540! That is almost double what I paid for it, and it is almost the MSRP of the 9070XT which is a monumentally better card according to benchmarks.

Anyway, madness out there. Thankfully I am no longer a gamer so that I don't have to deal with this now. Even now that I have much more money, I still feel bad buying these cards as I feel scammed. Sorry for y'all gamers.

Your comment about not using these cards for 4K is misleading NONSENSE. You do NOT have to play games at "ultra" settings for them to look great. "Ultra" is a setting that NOBODY should use in the first few years of a game, as it's very specifically designed for future hardware and has vastly diminishing returns. Meanwhile, consoles tend to match "medium" settings, and those still look great. Even "low" is often totally fine.

Benchmarks at "ultra" settings are useful for comparing hardware, but it's WRONG to assume that people play that way or should play that way.

Don't miss out on 4K due to bad advice from YouTubers who spend all day benchmarking and forget what it's like to actually play! 4K is absolutely within reach of newer entry-level GPUs.

comments.text:
To be fair, I recently built a computer for my daughter, using older spare parts I had lying around. She is currently using a GTX 970 which is a "4" GB card notorious for only having 3.5 GB of vRAM that gets the full performance. She's not playing very many demanding games, plays at 1920*1080@60hz, and doesn't mind running lower settings than the rest of us with 3080s/3090s in our systems, nor does she care about any RTX features she's missing. I recently swapped in my old GTX 1080 (8GB card) in place of my RTX 3090 to see how it ran 3440*1440@175hz and it did alright. I certainly wasn't actually achieving 175 fps, but it could reasonably manage ~60 fps at low-medium settings. Curiosity settled, I obviously switched back, but you can definitely still game at 8GB on a budget and even 4GB if you don't mind low settings at low resolutions in titles that aren't extremely demanding on GPUs and vRAM.

And to address the obvious response "why don't you let your daughter use your GTX 1080," it's a water-cooled card meant for custom loops. Her system is old spare parts I had lying around that need to be inter-compatible and I don't have enough spare pumps/rads/blocks/etc to complete the loop. The fastest air-cooled cards I still have are the GTX 970 and the R9 290X. The 970 is a slightly more "mature" card from a time when nVidia had much better drivers and power efficiency than AMD and she prefers nVidia's feel from that era. To be fair, she's probably getting a video card upgrade for Christmas, but I haven't yet decided which card to go with. I used to only buy ATI Radeon cards until the R9 290X (which I loved that card), but after my experience with the GTX 970, I switched entirely to nVidia. I want nothing to do with this generation of nVidia cards and don't see a reason to buy older cards when I can easily afford a newer one, so I'm considering switching back to AMD Radeon for the 9000 series or even giving Intel Arc a shot. We'll see what makes the most sense over the coming months.

comments.text:
For $299, the RTX 5060 does have a use albeit a very niche one that only some people (like myself) care about.

While it’s undeniably a bad value for gaming, the 5060 actually makes sense if you get it at MSRP and use it as a dedicated encoder/rendering GPU in a multi-GPU setup. The upgraded NVENC supports AV1 encoding, better H.264/H.265 performance, and improved efficiency over older generations. For anyone still pursuing multi-GPU workflows like offloading streaming, recording, or rendering tasks (in OBS, for example) the 5060 can fully take that load off your main GPU.

With SLI dead, using a second GPU for encoding is one of the few practical multi-GPU setups left and the 5060 fits that role well.

I'm currently running a 3080 Ti paired with a 3050 for exactly this reason. I'm skipping both the 40 and 50 series entirely, and waiting for the 60 series. When that drops, I’ll probably do the same thing again pair a 6080 with a 6060 for dedicated rendering and encoding.

So yeah... the 5060 sucks for gaming. But for light production work, or even desk setups with a bunch of monitors, it has some value. Plug your displays into the 5060, and let your main GPU (like a 5080 or 5090) handle everything else.

All I’m saying is there are use cases for the 5060. Even if they’re niche.

comments.text: Here's the thing. Looking at the Steam Hardware and software survey. Top display resolution, 1080p at 55.27%. Top VRAM 8GB at near 5%.  The next largest is 12GB. 1440p makes up around 23% and 4K is down around 5%.  Now, pricing matters of course. I didn't move over to 1440p until a year ago. I was running two 1080p monitors and switched to a single 1440p. Honestly, for gaming, the 1080p monitors were fine. At that resolution 8GB is fine as well. Now, moving beyond gaming, if you're a creator then 4k might make sense because you're probably rocking monitors greater than 30 inches. That's going to require a pretty high-end card. I run a 4070 super now and it runs all the games/sims I like in 1440p. Will I ever go to 4k on my PC? Probably not. Not a need and sure isn't worth the prices we are seeing now. So, just saying we can hate on NVidia if we like, but for the 1080p gaming crowd, which is still the majority, it's not a bad upgrade if you can get it at MSRP. Good luck with all that.

comments.author: @TheCrazyCanuck420

comments.text: The memory is chosen to keep the processing elements fed.  So they can't add memory willy-nilly like you can in a PC because the memory controllers are paired up to the compute units (cluster of PEs).  A wider memory bus usually comes with more CUs which means you get into 5070/5080 territory with a wider bus.  Not that I would buy this POS GPU, but my biggest concern would be the game assets fitting in such a low amount of VRAM.
comments.author: @TheCrazyCanuck420

comments.text: ​​ @TheCrazyCanuck420  Thanks for the info, good to learn new things 👍
comments.author: @peterwstacey

comments.text:
​​ @peterwstacey Sort of.  What I'm saying is, if the GPU had say 4 compute units with 32-bit memory controllers, you are stuck with that architecture and so if you use 2GiB memories you have 8GB.  You can scale that to 16GiB of memory using 4GiB memories which is what Jay is eluding to at the end of this video.  Nvidia, AMD, Intel all do a lot of simulations to figure out what the right amount and width of RAM to pair up to the compute side of the GPU otherwise money will be wasted on too much memory bandwidth, or too much compute and not enough memory bandwidth to keep it fed.  Then they just scale the compute hardware to create different GPU SKUs.  So of you take the compute of a 5070 and divide it by the 5060 number, you should see roughly the same ratio because more compute requires more memory bandwidth (plus the other compute units have very low speed access to the other CU memory controllers).

If you search around for the block diagrams of the 5xxx series you'll see what I mean about memory controllers pairing up to CU.  When you compare the 5060 to a 5070 for example, the 5060 will look like the 5070 with one side chopped off.  The 5060 is most likely a cut down 5070 die which might be a cut down 5080.

comments.text: I know this likely makes me sound like an idiot but can someone please explain what the 95/99% stats mean on the performance charts?
comments.author: @SynysterDB

comments.text:
99% is the same thing as you may have seen 1% lows.  So say your FPS is 100, but your 1% lows are 80, that means you're getting drops to 80fps.  Not always a big deal, but if you're getting 45fps to start and your 1% lows are 30, you're likely to feel that as stutters.  It really is hard to look at 1% lows without a frametime graph though as it matters how often you drop to those lows, which is what the 95%/5% lows try to show, how often are you dropping to those lower framerates.

Best laymen's term explanation I can give and never feel dumb for asking to learn.  Maybe someone can explain better than I did.
